description: Six peoples from Rangpur, from different departments, united by one question: why does the drought NASA can see from orbit never reach our own farmers? As Team Nokkhotro, we built Krishi BONDHU AI, a voice-first advisory where farmers ask in Bangla or English and hear field-specific advice drawn from NASA data. We don't want to replace a farmer's experience. We want to strengthen it with climate intelligence, starting in our own backyard.
summary: Rafik, a real smallholder farmer in Rangpur, Bangladesh, must choose between thirsty Boro rice and low-water crops while NASA satellites can already see the drought coming, a signal that never reaches him. Krishi BONDHU AI breaks this "Orbital Paradox" with a working voice-first demo: a farmer taps a microphone, asks in Bangla or English "Will it rain in the next 3 days?", and hears field-specific advice built from NASA SMAP, GPM, MODIS, Landsat, ECOSTRESS, POWER, SRTM and MERRA-2 data. Six domain agents and a master synthesis engine work over 1.91 million harmonized records (1980-2026, all 536 unions of Rangpur Division) to drive two Field Shifts: drought-hardy crops (45%-70% estimated water saved) and night irrigation at 3:30-6:00 AM to cut evaporation and diesel use. Because it runs on global NASA data, the pipeline is designed to be re-pointed to farmers in any climate-vulnerable region.
details:
THE CHALLENGE: THE "ORBITAL PARADOX"

Meet Rafik, a real smallholder farmer in Rangpur, whose struggle is shared by farmers in climate-vulnerable regions worldwide. In March he studies dry topsoil and must choose between high-risk Boro paddy and low-water crops. At midday, above 38 C, his 4 HP diesel pump burns fuel at 108 BDT/liter, and over 40% of the water evaporates before reaching the roots. In July, upstream surges in the Teesta and Brahmaputra basins can flood crops days before harvest.

Meanwhile, NASA satellites can detect drought weeks before the soil visibly cracks. The data exists (SMAP, Landsat 8/9, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, GPM) but is locked in NetCDF4, HDF5 and GeoTIFF granules, at resolutions that do not match farm plots, and behind language barriers. That gap is the Orbital Paradox.

The stakes (per our research baseline): Boro paddy needs 2,500-5,000 liters of water per kg of grain; in the Barind Tract and Teesta basin groundwater falls each dry season and irrigation's share of farmer cost has risen from 12.3% to 37.5%.

OUR SOLUTION: TWO FIELD SHIFTS

Crop Shift: move from high-water crops to drought-hardy alternatives.

Irrigation Shift: move from daytime blind pumping to precision night irrigation (3:30-6:00 AM) guided by SMAP root moisture and GPM rain forecasts.

HOW IT WORKS

1) Data foundation. We harmonized a tabular dataset of 1,913,624 records for all 536 unions of Rangpur Division, 1980-2026 (564 monthly time-steps), in seven CSV files built by reproducible Python scripts, one per agent.

2) 6+1 Multi-Agent Architecture. Six domain agents ingest NASA and partner data; a master engine synthesizes them:

•     Agent 1, Precipitation and Flood: GPM IMERG and POWER rainfall plus BWDB river-gauge models; flood risk and 3-day rain warnings that tell farmers to hold the pump.

•     Agent 2, Thermal and Drought: MODIS land surface temperature and ECOSTRESS; evapotranspiration anomalies and stress flagged before stomata close.

•     Agent 3, Soil Hydrology: SMAP L4 root-zone moisture (0-100 cm) with BMDA groundwater logs.

•     Agent 4, Agronomy, Solar, Humidity: Landsat 8/9 and MODIS NDVI/EVI plus POWER irradiance and humidity; canopy vigour and fungal blight risk.

•     Agent 5, Farmer Priority and Economy: NASA stress flags plus FAO GAEZ, World Bank CPI and DAM prices across 22 crops to optimize net profit per hectare (BDT/ha); prices CPI-deflated over 47 years.

•     Agent 6, Atmosphere and Wind: MERRA-2 and POWER pressure, humidity and wind; squall (Kalbaishakhi) and lodging alerts.

•     +1 Master Synthesis Engine: resolves conflicts between agents (e.g. high profit vs flash-flood risk) into a multi-season rotation and night-irrigation schedule. SRTM (30 m) adds union elevation, slope and runoff.

Answers are designed to be grounded in these stored datasets and explicit formulas (water demand, pump runtime, fuel and power cost), so each figure traces to a source.

3) AgroBani voice-first UI. Bangla (bn-BD) and English (en-US) via the Web Speech API; 80 px microphone button for muddy hands, question chips and text fallback for windy fields. It answers rain, soil moisture, pump cost and crop questions, with one-tap replay. Also: SVG parcel explorer (SMAP, NDVI, ECOSTRESS, GPM layers), crop shift matrix, pump cost calculator with a 7-day rain-aware calendar, printable field report. Built for entry-level Android (48x48 px targets, dark mode, 16123 helpline link).

IMPACT (CROP-MATRIX ESTIMATES, NOT FIELD TRIALS)

•     Crop Shift saves 45%-70% of water: pearl millet about 60% (matures in 75-85 days vs 140 for paddy), sorghum about 45%, chickpeas/pulses about 70% and fix 40-60 kg N/ha, cutting urea cost about 50%.

•     Irrigation Shift targets evaporative loss; our dashboard scenario shows 38.5% water conserved.

 

LIMITATIONS

Impact figures are crop-matrix estimates and dashboard values are demonstration data. Our dataset covers Rangpur today, so other regions need local data and calibration.

NEXT STEPS

- Validate on the ground: pilot with DAE extension officers in Rangpur, comparing the advice with field observations.

- Scale globally: re-point the master grid to any region (the NASA sources are global) and add local partner data and crop profiles.

- Widen crop coverage beyond the current 22-crop matrix. - Add predictive market models that forecast profit per hectare from the CPI-deflated price history.


Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We used AI tools as a supportive resource throughout the project. Specifically:

1. Scikit-learn (Random Forest): a traditional machine learning model, not generative AI. It runs inside our agents' logic to support crop suitability, drought stress and flood-risk advisories. It works on our harmonized NASA dataset (MODIS, GPM, SMAP, etc.) for Rangpur Division.

2. Claude Code and Claude: coding assistants for writing boilerplate code, data cleaning scripts (NaN and -999 values) and bug fixes. They worked on our own project code and public NASA data scripts.

3. Claude and Google Gemini: content tools for drafting the README, project text and video script, and for Bangla/English phrasing. They worked only on our own project text. Validation: our team manually reviewed and tested all AI-generated code and facts, and checked NASA mission claims against official NASA documentation. Farmer advice comes from the data-driven models, not from a generative AI guessing. No personal data was entered into AI tools.
